results.title: Reproducible Builds | Brandon Mitchell
results.content: Most reproducible build implementations now are focused on a single part of the builder step. This requires a lot of work by developers to make the build tooling reproducible, often done by running the build inside of pinned containers. For builders that don’t, reproducible build tooling needs to wrap the build in a way that isolates the build and prevents inputs from accessing signing keys or compromising the builder. Tooling is only half the reason we aren’t all building artifacts reproducible builders and verifying those builds. There’s an added expense to implementing reproducible builders because each build multiplies the CPU time and other expenses to run the build infrastructure. The tooling needs to be updated to support those reproducible builds and make implementations cheaper. A government requirement for verified reproducible builds would change the financial equation that drives business decisions. In my own projects, I’ve been working on improving the tooling around reproducible builds for container images.

results.title: Automated, Reproducible and Secure Development & CI ...
results.content: # Automated, Reproducible and Secure Development & CI environments: Package Management (1/3). Nix Flakes can be used to run **development shells** (among lots of great things like create container images or install full-blown OS with NixOS)². Nix also generates a `flake.lock` we can version along with `flake.nix`, thus ensuring **reproducibility**: next time we or anyone else runs `nix develop`, they'll have exactly the same packages installed. It's frequent to couple application package managers with other solutions like Docker or Nix to ensure better reproducibility. Application package manager by themselves probably won't be able to provide a sufficient layer of automation and reproducibility, leaving you with a consequent amount of manual setup and drift between developers and CI environment. Application package managers are the basics of development environment setup, but far from enough to ensure proper automation and reproducibility. Container (e.g Docker) images can provide a development environment by running a shell in container directly.

results.title: The Appearance of Intelligence: How LLM-Skew and Retconned History Corrode Engineering Practice | by Robert Anderson | Medium
results.content:
Title: The Appearance of Intelligence: How LLM-Skew and Retconned History Corrode Engineering Practice | by Robert Anderson | Medium
• Templates (the how): parameterised generation units. • Manifests (the what): declarative specs of components, dependencies, versions, policies. • Provenance (the why/when): decision records, changelogs, tagged artefacts. • Reproducibility (the test): rebuild from templates + manifests; verify hashes, outputs, and contracts. • T0 (primary) – dated artefact of the period: code/tag/patch, DDL, RFC, release note, mailing-list post. • T2 (secondary) – later retrospectives that reference T0/T1. • T3 (marketing) – claims without verifiable artefacts. • /docs/history.md – append-only, dated entries; link to tags, migrations, ADRs. • /docs/adr/ADR-YYYYMMDD-<slug>.md – one architectural decision per file (context, alternatives, consequences). • CHANGELOG.md – append-only; reference semantic versions and migration scripts. • MANIFEST.\* – declarative component list (versions, checksums, policies). • TEMPLATES/ – generator units; no business logic embedded in ad-hoc scripts. • BUILD/ – reproducible build scripts with pinned toolchains and deterministic flags. • ADR link for new or changed architecture. • “List earliest primary sources (≤ YEAR) with dates; separate claims (summary) from evidence (links/tags/RFC numbers).”. • “If no primary source exists ≤ YEAR, return ‘unverified’ – do not substitute later summaries.”. • “Compare earliest source to a later whitepaper; return a diff of materially changed claims.”. • Process: pure function from (manifest, template, policy) → artefacts. • Outputs: artefacts + provenance (hashes, manifest digest, template version, policy digest). • Agent patches directly in the repo without updating the manifest or template. • Evidence tier for each architectural claim (T0/T1 required). • Changelog updated, linked to tag/release. • SBOM generated and stored with build artefacts. • Prompts separate claims/evidence with date cutoffs. • All artefacts generated from versioned templates. • Manifests are the single source of truth. • Outputs include checksums of inputs (manifest/template/policy). • Explainable: each artefact traces to a manifest row and template version. • Portable: manifests and templates are platform-agnostic; execution targets are pluggable. • Accepting changes that lack an ADR and manifest delta. • Allowing agents to “fix” code directly in place without updating templates. • The antidote isn’t hype; it’s discipline: templates, manifests, provenance, and reproducible builds enforced by policy. • If you can re-generate the system from its specs and get the same guarantees, you have intelligence.
